purpose: Ledgerline PR3, 'Your data': a stranger can bring their own data. They read how to prepare CSV files, upload them into a private workspace, get a pass/fail Check with the exact fix for every problem, confirm which fields the model may see, then ask questions in plain English and see the SQL. It runs locally in this PR; hosting comes in PR5.
mechanism:
1. ledgerline/workspace/store.py keeps each workspace in its own folder under the data directory: an id from secrets (128 bits) sent in a header, states new -> checked -> confirmed, every change under one per-workspace lock that re-reads metadata, and disk reservations under one global lock. Delete removes the folder (moved to .trash first); `ledgerline sweep` removes workspaces idle for 7 days.
2. ledgerline/workspace/limits.py: per-IP rate limits for uploads and asks, at most 3 live workspaces per IP, a global disk cap, and X-Forwarded-For used only when LEDGERLINE_TRUST_PROXY=1 (right-most value across every header line). Uploads are a raw PUT body streamed with a size limit.
3. ledgerline/workspace/rules.py and check.py implement the Prepare-your-data rules (encoding and BOM, delimiter, headers and their slugs, ID columns named id, <table>_id or <singular>_id, link columns <x>_id to table x or xs, null spellings, ISO dates and datetimes, plain numbers with ASCII digits only, leading zeros keep text, limits on columns, rows and cell length). Messages name file, row, column and fix, capped at 20 per file. Columns are typed in order: ID columns from their values, links from the target ID's type, then the rest. A column named after its own table is one of its ID names, never a link.
4. ledgerline/workspace/load.py builds the SQLite database in a staging folder and swaps it in only on success, so a refused Check changes nothing.
5. ledgerline/workspace/fields.py drafts the registry for Confirm: hide or unhide fields, add descriptions, and opt in per column to share its values with the model. ledgerline/pipeline/prompt.py has one renderer used by both the Confirm preview and the interpret prompt.
6. ledgerline/workspace/ask.py runs the existing pipeline against the workspace: its own registry, read-only executor and audit log (audit.sqlite inside the folder). Relative dates use the wall clock in the workspace's time zone; evals keep the pinned reference time. Refusals are plain English. With no live model the API answers 503 'Live answers need a model key; see the README.'
7. ledgerline/workspace/api.py and ledgerline/api.py expose the routes; creating a workspace requires a JSON request. The pages in web/ (Prepare, Upload, Check, Confirm, Ask) are a Vite + TypeScript build served by FastAPI; user strings are inserted as text; stale responses are ignored.
8. verify.sh and CI build the pages and run eight Playwright tests plus the Python suite with per-module coverage floors.
decisions:
- Local first: hosting, the invite gate and a live key come in PR5, so the upload code is reviewed on its own.
- Category values reach the model only when the user opts in, because they leave the machine.
- The workspace id travels in a header and the bookmark #fragment, never the URL path, so it stays out of logs and Referer headers.
- No new runtime dependency: streamed PUT uploads instead of multipart, and an in-process rate limiter that resets on restart.
- Check and Load agree by construction and by a property test; a refused Check leaves the last good state.
- Self-links are not detected: a column named after its own table is an ID name. A future 'links to' choice on Confirm could add them.
- Deferred to PR5: disk-cap accounting can overshoot by a few KB and does not count temp files left by a crash.
readers: README.md -> people trying or evaluating the project (recruiters, developers who clone it); the Prepare page text -> people preparing their data; docs/adr/ -> engineers who want the reasoning; code comments -> the next maintainer. Cristian's rule: every comment, description and doc line deliberate, plain short sentences, terms defined on first use, no jargon-heavy decision prose.

docMap.behavior: Workspaces: create, upload, check, confirm, ask, delete, sweep
Confirm: hidden fields, descriptions, opt-in category values, shared prompt preview
Ask on a workspace: wall-clock dates, plain refusals, no-key reply
verify.sh and CI run the browser tests
